name: Grape seed extract

card.summary: A grape-derived procyanidin antioxidant; the appearance case rests on lab data, with no trials on skin or looks.
card.note: Forum aromatase claim comes from cell and mouse studies only.

quick.overview:
Grape seed extract is a supplement made from grape seeds, rich in procyanidin polyphenols. It is sold for antioxidant and vascular support and appears in some skin products.

Human trials are small and look at blood pressure, lipids and exercise rather than appearance. Looksmaxxing forum interest centres on a laboratory finding that it inhibits aromatase.
quick.mechanism: Procyanidins scavenge free radicals in laboratory tests and inhibited aromatase and digestive enzymes in cell studies. Absorption of the larger oligomers is limited in animal work.
quick.risks: Reported effects are mild (stomach upset, headache) according to secondary sources, with possible interactions with anticoagulants. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US. Effects on estrogen in humans have not been published.

lead: Grape seed extract (GSE) is a dietary supplement made from the seeds of grapes, mainly Vitis vinifera, which are a by-product of winemaking and grape-juice production. Its polyphenol fraction, typically 5-8% of the seed by weight, consists largely of flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin and their oligomers and polymers, known as procyanidins or oligomeric proanthocyanidin complexes (OPCs).[1][2]

It is sold as oral capsules and as an ingredient in topical products, and is marketed for antioxidant, vascular and skin-related purposes.[3][4] The appearance case runs through a chain: antioxidant polyphenols, possible support for blood vessels and skin, and, in some forum discussions, lower estrogen conversion that users link to a leaner, less puffy look.[5] In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in discussions of skin health and of aromatase inhibition, a claim drawn from laboratory studies.[5]

Published human trials of GSE are generally small and have examined outcomes such as blood pressure, cholesterol, vascular stiffness and exercise performance; a 2007 dermatology review lists it among botanicals used or proposed for skin care, but no published trial tests it for appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or skin tone.[3][6][7] Much of the biological work comes from cell and animal studies.[2][3]

chain: Antioxidant activity and, in cell studies, aromatase inhibition
Claimed: healthier-looking skin and less estrogen conversion
angle.text: Users take GSE hoping for healthier skin and, in the case of the aromatase claim, a drier, leaner look from lower estrogen. The mechanism comes from laboratory studies; human appearance outcomes have not been published.

paras: Grape seeds contain lipids, protein, carbohydrate and roughly 5-8% polyphenols depending on variety. The polyphenols are mainly gallic acid, monomeric flavan-3-ols (catechin, epicatechin, gallocatechin, epigallocatechin and epicatechin gallate) and procyanidin dimers, trimers and larger polymers.[2] Commercial extracts are generally standardised to a procyanidin percentage; Wikipedia describes classic extraction with organic solvents such as acetone, methanol and ethyl acetate, and notes that hot water is less effective.[9]

Wikipedia's proanthocyanidin article lists grape seeds at about 3,532 mg per 100 g among the richest dietary sources, alongside cinnamon bark and baking chocolate, and notes that a Procyanidolic Index of 95 on product labels was wrongly read as 95% procyanidin content, with current methods suggesting actual content is much lower.[8] Procyanidin C1, a trimer present in small amounts, has been studied separately in cell and mouse experiments.[10]

GSE is marketed as an antioxidant and for vascular health. NCCIH says it is sold as a supplement often to lower blood cholesterol and blood pressure, and appears in topical products for wound healing and in mouthrinses.[4] Some topical and oral products pair it with other ingredients; one US-listed bruise-support product combines GSE with arnica, bromelain, vitamin C, rutin and zinc oxide and states that it reduces pain, swelling and discolouration from bruises.[11] The evidence behind that combination is the manufacturer's statement, not a published trial of GSE alone.

A 2007 Dermatologic Therapy review of botanical cosmeceuticals names grape seed extract among botanicals used or showing promise for dermatologic purposes, alongside rosemary, propolis, oatmeal and olive oil.[6] A 2006 review of chemoprevention of nonmelanoma skin cancer lists polyphenolic antioxidants found in green tea and grape seed extract among potential agents.[12] These reviews describe candidate uses; they do not report trials of GSE on wrinkles or complexion.

Cochrane reviews of phlebotonics, a class of oral and topical agents used for chronic venous insufficiency, have been published in 2005, 2016 and 2020; they assess drugs such as rutosides, diosmin and calcium dobesilate for leg symptoms such as pain, swelling and tiredness.[13][14]

In laboratory work, grape seed polyphenols scavenge free radicals and inhibit lipid peroxidation.[2] Extracts have also inhibited the digestive enzymes alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase in vitro.[15] Wikipedia notes that proanthocyanidins have low bioavailability, with about 90% going unabsorbed until gut bacteria metabolise them.[8] Procyanidin oligomers have been absorbed and metabolised in animal studies, and absorption of procyanidin dimers and trimers has been examined in rats and in food-matrix models.[16][17]

Aromatase is the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into estrogens, and aromatase inhibitors lower estrogen; they are mainly used in hormone-sensitive breast cancer and are sometimes used off-label by men managing estrogen during testosterone therapy, according to Wikipedia.[18] A laboratory paper shared on looksmax.org reports that a grape seed extract rich in procyanidin dimers inhibited aromatase activity in a dose-dependent way, reduced tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model using aromatase-transfected breast cancer cells, and lowered aromatase mRNA levels in two breast cancer cell lines.[5] The work was done in cell lines and mice; no human data on the effect were presented in that thread.

A 2021 Nature Metabolism paper reported that procyanidin C1, a flavonoid from grape seed extract, had senotherapeutic activity in cells and increased lifespan in mice.[10] Interest in this finding in longevity and skin-aging circles is a cell-and-mouse result and has not been tested in a skin appearance trial.

Wikipedia credits the French researcher Jacques Masquelier with the discovery of proanthocyanidins in 1947 and says he patented extraction methods for pine bark and grape seeds.[8] The supplement industry later marketed the resulting extracts as OPCs. A 2002 safety evaluation of a proanthocyanidin-rich grape seed extract in toxicology models and a 2003 review of grape seed polyphenol biochemistry became widely cited references for the material.[2][19]

NCCIH states that grape seed extract is generally well tolerated when taken orally or applied to the skin, and that little is known about safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding; it advises people on medicines to talk to a provider, since some herbs and drugs interact.[4] Wikipedia lists itchy scalp, dizziness, headache and nausea as possible side effects, and notes well-tolerated oral use over 14 weeks in one study.[9] Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, reports possible interactions with anticoagulants and cytochrome P450 substrates; this is unverified secondary information.[1] A 2002 toxicology study evaluated a proanthocyanidin-rich extract.[19]

Wikipedia reports that grape seed extract has been promoted on social media as a cancer cure, that no clinical evidence shows it works against cancer, and that the US FDA listed it among fake cancer cures in 2017.[9] The article also cites a 2022 AFP fact-check and a 2024 statement from Cancer Council Australia.[9] Dietary supplements are not approved by the FDA before sale; manufacturers are responsible for safety and labelling.[4]

On looksmax.org, GSE is mentioned mainly as a possible natural aromatase inhibitor, based on a laboratory paper shared in a forum thread. Replies in that thread warned that lowering estrogen too far is a concern.[5] The supplement is sold over the counter in capsule form, as part of skin and vascular blends, and as a cosmetic ingredient.[3][4]

A 2016 meta-analysis of 16 trials, summarised on Wikipedia, found that doses under 800 mg per day for at least 8 weeks may lower systolic and diastolic blood pressure, with a larger effect of about 8.5 mmHg systolic in people with metabolic syndrome; the authors noted small, varied studies and called for larger trials.[9] NCCIH reports a 2020 review of 11 small studies suggesting possible benefits for LDL cholesterol and triglycerides but not total or HDL cholesterol, and a 2022 review of 19 studies finding reductions in diastolic but not systolic blood pressure.[4] A 2021 randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy volunteers examined a standardised extract and blood pressure and perceived stress.[7]

Registered human studies have examined estrogen levels in postmenopausal women, blood pressure in pre-hypertension, lipid profile and oxidised LDL in hyperlipidaemia, arterial stiffness in obese adults, muscle metaboreflex and cycling performance, and PSA in prostate cancer patients.[20][21][22][23][24] A dental trial has tested GSE as a collagen cross-linker before veneer bonding.[25] The postmenopausal estrogen study (NCT00566553, n=39) was listed as completed in 2008, and no published results were located.[20] No studies found on appearance outcomes such as wrinkles, skin elasticity or facial aesthetics.

timeline.event: Jacques Masquelier discovers proanthocyanidins, according to Wikipedia.[8]
A safety evaluation of a proanthocyanidin-rich grape seed extract is published in Food and Chemical Toxicology.[19]
A Journal of Medicinal Food review covers the biochemistry and functionality of grape seed polyphenols.[2]
A registered trial of GSE on estrogen levels in postmenopausal women begins.[20]
A meta-analysis of 16 trials examines GSE and blood pressure.[9]
The FDA lists grape seed extract among fake cancer cures, per Wikipedia.[9]
A meta-analysis reports possible reductions in LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, triglycerides and C-reactive protein.[9]
Procyanidin C1 is reported to have senotherapeutic activity and extend lifespan in mice.[10]
A review of 19 studies finds lower diastolic but not systolic blood pressure, per NCCIH.[4]
Cancer Council Australia issues a statement on grape seed extract cancer claims.[9]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, GSE is mentioned mainly as a possible natural aromatase inhibitor, based on a laboratory paper shared in a forum thread.[5]

claims.claim: Grape seed extract works as an aromatase inhibitor and so can lower estrogen.
claims.believers: A forum poster shared a laboratory paper showing GSE inhibited aromatase activity in cell and xenograft models and presented it as a supplement route to reducing estrogen conversion; replies cautioned about lowering estrogen too far.[5]
claims.experts: The cited work is a laboratory and mouse-xenograft study in breast cancer models.[5] A registered human trial has examined GSE's effect on estrogen levels in postmenopausal women, and no published results were located.[20]

claims.claim: GSE improves skin health and appearance through its antioxidant polyphenols.
claims.believers: Marketing and some users describe OPCs as antioxidants that support skin and blood vessels.[3]
claims.experts: A 2007 review lists GSE among botanicals used for skin;[6] laboratory studies show free-radical scavenging,[2] and no trial has tested wrinkles or skin tone.

claims.claim: GSE lowers blood pressure and supports circulation.
claims.believers: Supplement sellers promote it for vascular and blood-pressure support.[4]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report possible blood-pressure reductions in small, varied trials, with a 2022 review finding diastolic but not systolic effects.[4][9]

claims.claim: GSE helps with bruises and swelling.
claims.believers: A US-listed bruise-support product containing GSE states it reduces pain, swelling and discolouration.[11]
claims.experts: The product combines several ingredients and no published trial of GSE alone for bruises was found.[11]

claims.believers: Social-media posts have promoted it as a cancer cure.[9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says no clinical evidence shows it is effective against cancer and that the FDA listed it among fake cancer cures in 2017.[9]

claims.claim: GSE slows skin aging through senescent-cell effects.
claims.believers: Longevity-minded users point to procyanidin C1 results.[10]
claims.experts: The 2021 paper tested cells and mice; no human trial of GSE on aging skin was found.[10]
